pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 8–9 (UK Y4, US Grade 3–4). Counting in 6s, 7s, 9s, 25s and 1,000s — the harder skip counts that complete the times-table set and extend into thousands.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25 and 1,000', 'find 1,000 more or less than a given number', and 'count backwards through 0 to include negative numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.7 fluent recall of products (the 6s, 7s, 9s underpin those tables); 4.OA.5 generate and analyse number/shape patterns; 4.NBT reading/place value into the thousands.
• Operational details: exploit structure so these are not brute memorised — 6s = doubled 3s; 9s carry a strong pattern (tens digit +1 while ones digit −1 each step, digit sum always 9, a clean diagonal on the hundred square); 7s have the WEAKEST pattern so need the most rehearsal, best built from 5s+2s; 25s are quarters/money/quarter-hours (four 25s = 100); 1,000s extend the place-value step and pair with backward counting through 0 into negatives.
• Checkpoint: skip-count and use structure to self-repair. Tier A (8): count in 6s and 25s from 0 and count in 1,000s. Tier B (8–9): count in 6s, 7s, 9s, 25s, 1,000s from 0 and find 1,000 more/less. Tier C (9): explain 6s as doubled 3s and use the 9s digit pattern (digit sum 9) to check a count, and count in 1,000s backwards through 0 into negatives.
bestPractices: Lead with structure, not brute rote: teach 6s as doubled 3s, and surface the 9s pattern explicitly (each step the tens digit rises by one and the ones digit falls by one, so the digits always sum to 9) so children have a self-check when a count wobbles.

Give the 7s the most rehearsal because they carry the weakest visible pattern — build them from known 5s and 2s (7 = 5 + 2) and from the array, and interleave them with already-secure counts rather than drilling in isolation.
Anchor 25s in quarters and money — four 25s make 100, 25p pieces, quarter-hours — so 25, 50, 75, 100 is felt as building whole hundreds from quarters rather than a memorised list.
Connect every count to its times table and to equal groups/arrays so counting in 6s, 7s and 9s is the fluency route into the ×6, ×7 and ×9 facts, not a parallel skill.

Teach 1,000s alongside 1,000-more/less and backward counting through 0 into negatives, using a number line that extends past 0 so the place-value step and the negative extension are seen on one continuous track.
keyRepresentations: Hundred square with the 9s shaded to reveal the diagonal and the digit-sum-9 pattern (and 6s to show doubled 3s)
Aligned number lines pairing 3s with 6s (doubling) and 5s+2s composing 7s
Equal groups / arrays for 6, 7, 9 linking each count to its multiplication table
Money and clock models for 25s (four quarters = 100, quarter-hours) and an extended number line through 0 for 1,000s and negatives
commonMisconceptions: Counting in 7s (and 6s/9s) as pure rote with no structural anchor, so a single slip cannot be repaired and the count derails.
Missing the 9s pattern and treating each step as '+10 then −1' incorrectly, e.g. writing 9, 18, 27, 37 by adding 10 and forgetting the −1.
Confusing adjacent tables (drifting between 6s and 8s, or 7s and 9s) because the steps feel similar and no pattern flags the error.
Mishandling 25s past 100 (25, 50, 75, 100, 125 becoming …100, 105) by reverting to a smaller or rounder step at the hundred.
Counting in 1,000s but stalling or reversing sign incorrectly when crossing 0 into negatives (…1000, 0, then '1000' again instead of −1000).

learn.summary: Skip counting in6s,7s,9s,25s and1,000s for ages8–9 uses equal groups and number patterns. Build6-jumps from two3-jumps,7-jumps from5+2,25s from four25-unit parts making100, and1,000s on a line through zero. For9,18,…,90 the digits sum to9 and the tens-up/ones-down pattern is visible; it does not extend unchanged to99, whose digits sum to18. Use patterns as checks within their stated range.

activities.title: Step the count and watch the pattern form (pattern explorer)
feedback: For a term in the9-through90 segment, check the tens and ones sum to9. Do not mark99 wrong because its sum is18:99 is also a multiple of9. Beyond that segment, verify the jump or multiplication fact rather than requiring digit sum exactly9.
A common slip is applying '+10' alone (9, 18, 27, 37); point out the missing −1 on the ones digit and that 37's digits sum to 10, not 9.
If the 7s stall, rebuild the next term from the previous one plus 5 plus 2, or derive 7×6 from 7×5+7 (= 35 + 7 = 42) rather than counting on in ones.
At the hundred boundary in 25s (75 → 100 → 125), check the step stayed 25 and did not shrink to a rounder jump such as +5.
When crossing 0 in the 1,000s count, note the sign flips once: ...2000, 1000, 0, −1000, −2000 — not 1000 again.
activities.rationale: Optional controls can shade each multiple and display its actual digit sum. Show the9-through90 tens-up/ones-down pattern, then display99 with digit sum18 rather than keeping a false locked9 meter. Other optional views pair two3-jumps per6-jump,5+2 per7-jump,25-unit parts to100, and1,000-unit jumps across zero.
sourceClaims: Year 4: count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25 and 1,000; find 1,000 more or less than a given number; count backwards through 0 to include negative numbers.
The 9s times table shows a digit-sum-of-9 / tens-up-ones-down pattern used as a self-check; 6s are taught as doubled 3s; 7s carry the weakest pattern and need most rehearsal.
learnerActions: Pick a count (6s, 7s, 9s, 25s, or 1,000s) and step it one jump at a time, saying each multiple aloud.

Step0,9,18,…,90. From9 to90, treat9 as09 if comparing tens and ones: the tens digit rises by1, the ones falls by1, and the digit sum is9. Then inspect99: its digits sum to18, so the earlier pattern does not continue unchanged.
For the 6s, show each 6-jump as two 3-jumps (the jump 0→6 is 3+3, and the jump 6→12 is a further 3+3), so each multiple of 6 is reached by pairs of 3-jumps.
For the 7s, build each step as a 5-jump plus a 2-jump (7 = 5 + 2) and rebuild any forgotten term that way.
For25s, partition a100-unit bar or collection into four equal25-unit parts, then continue25,50,75,100,125,150. A quarter-hour clock uses15-minute steps to60, so do not use it to label25-unit steps.
For the 1,000s, step along a number line that continues through 0 into negatives, and find 1,000 more or 1,000 less of a given number.
activities.intendedInsight: Use patterns within a stated range:9 through90 have digit sum9, while99 has digit sum18; each6-jump is two3-jumps;7-jumps can be5+2; four25-unit parts make100; and1,000-unit steps continue through zero.

activities.title: Hundred-square reference with reveal-on-tap structure
feedback: Confirm digit sums from the actual cell:18 through90 sum to9;99 sums to18 and is still a multiple of9. Ask which part of the earlier visual pattern changed.
Use the nested 3s to confirm a 6s term when unsure.
activities.rationale: A laid-out, tap-to-reveal reference surfaces the patterns and serves as a quick check. It does not let the learner generate the count or watch the digit pattern update step by step, so it works best as a reference alongside an activity where the learner drives the count.
sourceClaims: The 9s times table shows a digit-sum-of-9 / tens-up-ones-down pattern used as a self-check; 6s are taught as doubled 3s; 7s carry the weakest pattern and need most rehearsal.
learnerActions: Explore a hundred square with the multiples of 9 and the 6s pattern marked. On a 0–99 square, 9 through 90 form a diagonal. On a 1–100 square, 9 through 81 form the diagonal and 90 sits off it.
Reveal each multiple-of9 cell’s actual digits and sum. Compare18 through90, whose digits sum to9, with99, whose digits sum to18.
Reveal the two 3s nested inside a 6s cell.
Reveal the quarter or coin value behind a 25s cell.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference can show the9s pattern through90 and its change at99, alongside pairs of3-jumps within6-jumps and25-unit quarters of100. Check the actual values rather than extending a visual rule beyond its valid range.

activities.title: Check counts and table links
feedback: For a9s blank in the9-through90 segment, digit sum9 is a useful check. For99 or other ranges, verify the step or multiplication fact rather than requiring a sum of exactly9.
For 1,000 less than 4,200, confirm the answer is 3,200 (reduce the thousands digit by 1).
For the count through 0, confirm the next terms are −1000 and −2000, not a repeat of 1000.
For 'seven groups of 9', confirm 63 and relate it to the 9s count reaching 63 at the seventh step from 0.
activities.rationale: Short, varied questions check these counts and their table links and can surface the specific '+10 only' 9s error and the sign error when crossing 0. Checking is distinct from building the pattern insight, so this complements the generative activity rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Year 4: count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25 and 1,000; find 1,000 more or less than a given number; count backwards through 0 to include negative numbers.
3.OA.7 fluent recall of products (6s/7s/9s tables); 4.OA.5 generate and analyse number patterns.
learnerActions: Fill a missing term in a sequence, e.g. 6, 12, __, 24.
Fill a 9s blank where a wrong '+10 only' rule would give the wrong answer, then justify using the digit sum.
Match 'seven groups of 9' to 63 and similar table facts.
Continue a 1,000s sequence downward through 0 into negatives (e.g. 2000, 1000, 0, __, __).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent skip counts connect directly to multiplication facts and extend cleanly across the hundred and through 0, and can be checked using structure.

activities.title: Oral rehearsal partner for the weak 7s
feedback: If a 7s term is wrong, prompt rebuilding from the previous term plus 7, or from 5+2 jumps.
Reinforce short daily turns rather than one long chant.
activities.rationale: Spoken turn-taking rehearses the weakest-pattern 7s and prompts structural self-checks aloud. Because the key insight here is visual and structural, oral rehearsal supplements the generative pattern work; it is an oral-rehearsal affordance, not evidence that talk teaches the procedure better than other media.
sourceClaims: The 9s times table shows a digit-sum-of-9 / tens-up-ones-down pattern used as a self-check; 6s are taught as doubled 3s; 7s carry the weakest pattern and need most rehearsal.
learnerActions: Take turns counting in 7s aloud with a partner, each saying the next multiple.
When a term is forgotten, rebuild it from 5s + 2s or from a known fact (7×6 = 7×5 + 7 = 42) rather than counting on in ones.

When a 7s term is uncertain, check it by adding 7 to the previous term or by linking it to the matching ×7 fact (e.g. 7×4 = 28). The digit-sum-9 check belongs to the 9s count, not the 7s: 7s terms such as 14 or 28 do not have digit sum 9.
activities.intendedInsight: The hardest, least rhythmic count (7s) may become more reliable through short, frequent oral rehearsal paired with deriving forgotten terms from known facts.

constraints: Use number structure: pair3-jumps for6, compose5+2 for7, partition100 into four25-unit parts, and continue1,000-unit steps through zero. Scope the9s tens-up/ones-down and digit-sum9 pattern to9 through90;99 has digit sum18.
Give the 7s the most rehearsal because they carry the weakest visible pattern; interleave them with already-secure counts rather than drilling in isolation.
Connect every count to its times table and to equal groups/arrays so counting in 6s, 7s and 9s is the fluency route into ×6, ×7 and ×9, not a parallel skill.

A fixed/reference hundred square can reveal and confirm patterns but cannot let the learner generate the count or watch the digit pattern update step by step; use it as a reference, not the sole teaching vehicle.
Short check questions verify counts and table links but do not by themselves build the pattern insight; pair them with activities where the learner generates the count.
Do not respond to sub-counting by ones with more chanting alone; build fluency through retrieval — derive from known facts, use number-line jumps, and keep practice short and daily.
For the 1,000s crossing 0, the sign flips exactly once (…1000, 0, −1000, −2000); avoid repeating a positive term after 0.

The digit-sum9 check used here applies to9 through90, with9 written as09 for a tens/ones comparison. It does not apply unchanged to99; do not reject a correct multiple of9 just because its digits sum to18.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims for CCSS (3.OA.7/4.OA.5) and NCETM were marked verified:false in the original row; only the DfE National Curriculum claim was marked verified:true. Do not treat the unverified claims as established, including the '7s weakest pattern / most rehearsal' heuristic.

Self-audit of facts: 4 quarters = 100 (25, 50, 75, 100) is correct; 1,000 less than 4,200 = 3,200 is correct; 7×6 = 7×5 + 7 = 35 + 7 = 42 is correct; 7×9 = 63; counting 1,000s down through 0 gives 0, −1000, −2000 (sign flips once) — all consistent as used in activities.

Corrected a 6s illustration that previously read '12 = 6+6': that showed 12 as two 6-jumps, contradicting the stated 'two 3-jumps per 6-jump' mechanism. It now shows each 6-jump (0→6 and 6→12) as 3+3.

The original all-terms digit-sum9 rule was inaccurate:9 through90 show the stated pattern, but99 has digit sum18. The activities and reference-square feedback now expose that boundary rather than treating all two-digit multiples the same.

The original claim that these patterns 'read most clearly in flat 2D' and that a 3D scene 'adds nothing' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it has been dropped rather than asserted. A spatial/physical representation (e.g. a number line on the floor) may still support the negative-number extension.
'Count in steps of 1000 up to 10,000' from the evidence pairs with the negative extension; ensure the forward range and the backward-through-0 range are both practised.

probeDeeper: What's the next multiple of 7 after 56?
In the 9s, what do the tens and ones digits do as you go?
assess.correctAnswer: 0, 6, …, 72; 0, 7, …, 84; 0, 9, 18, …, 90; 0, 25, 50, …, 200; and notices in the 9s the tens digit rises while the ones falls (the digits sum to 9) — using pattern and known facts, not counting on by ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: sub-counts by ones — adds the group in single steps each time, most visibly on 7s: long pauses, finger counting, errors past 49
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT just demand more chanting — fluency comes from retrieval: derive from known facts (7×6 from 7×5+7), use number-line jumps, and keep practice short and daily
errorPatterns.revealedBy: slow, audible sub-counting; 7s markedly weaker than 6s

errorPatterns.pattern: misses the 9s pattern — counts the 9s laboriously without noticing the tens-up/ones-down structure (digits sum to 9)
errorPatterns.nextMove: list the 9s and ring the tens and ones digits to show the mirror pattern and digit-sum; hand it back as a self-check — the counting is there, the structure is the add-on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: no pattern-spotting even when prompted to watch the digits

errorPatterns.pattern: boundary/large-step slips — loses place in the 25s at hundred boundaries (75, 100) or miscounts the 1000s toward 10,000
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT reteach the whole sequence — link 25s to money/quarters and the hundred square, and rehearse the 75→100 and thousands bridges specifically
errorPatterns.revealedBy: boundary errors in the 25s or 1000s runs

responseLevels.gap: Cannot sustain 6s/7s/9s without counting every one in between; no use of pattern or known facts.
responseLevels.full: Skip-counts 6s, 7s, 9s, 25s, 1000s fluently by stepping the group size, and exploits structure (the 9s digit-sum, 25s as quarter-hundreds) to check and extend.
responseLevels.partial: Recites the more familiar sequences but sub-counts on 7s/9s and misses their structure (e.g. the 9s digit pattern).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count in 6s from 0 to 72. Now the hard one — count in 7s from 0 to 84. Then count in 9s to 90, and count in 25s to 200. As you do the 9s, watch the digits — do you notice anything? (Watch the 7s especially, sub-counting, and whether they spot the 9s tens-up/ones-down pattern.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 6s, 7s and 9s are the least rhythmic multiples and the classic fluency bottleneck (7s hardest), so this is the clearest test of pattern- and fact-based skip counting versus laborious sub-counting. A fluent child steps by the group size and leans on structure (the 9s digit pattern, 25s as quarter-hundreds); a struggling child counts on in ones between terms — reliably slower and error-prone on 7s.
